text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
note: Possibly the most famous opening line in English. Read it twice: it is stated as a universal truth, but it is really the neighbours who want the rich man, not the other way around. The voice of the whole novel is in this sentence.

text: …Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.
note: From the first page: the narrator explains why he goes to sea. It's a cure for melancholy, told as a joke. Notice how the “whenever” clauses pile up and build like a swell.

text: …Let the most absentminded of men be plunged in his deepest reveries—stand that man on his legs, set his feet a-going, and he will infallibly lead you to water, if water there be in all that region. Should you ever be athirst in the great American desert, try this experiment, if your caravan happen to be supplied with a metaphysical professor. Yes, as everyone knows, meditation and water are wedded forever.
note: Melville's half-comic theory that every human being is drawn to water. An early sign that this book will be as much philosophy as adventure.

text: …nothing contributes so much to tranquillise the mind as a steady purpose—a point on which the soul may fix its intellectual eye.
note: Written by the Arctic explorer whose letters frame the novel, before the main story begins. Ambition as a cure for restlessness: an idea the whole book will put to the test.

text: “Whenever you feel like criticizing anyone,” he told me, “just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.”
note: Advice from the narrator's father, on the first page. Nick says it taught him to reserve judgment. Keep an eye on whether he really does.

text: …Yet high over the city our line of yellow windows must have contributed their share of human secrecy to the casual watcher in the darkening streets, and I saw him too, looking up and wondering. I was within and without, simultaneously enchanted and repelled by the inexhaustible variety of life.
note: Nick, stuck at a loud party in a Manhattan apartment, imagines a stranger in the street looking up at the lit windows, and then feels like that stranger himself. A perfect sentence about watching your own life.

text: What a lark! What a plunge! For so it had always seemed to her, when, with a little squeak of the hinges, which she could hear now, she had burst open the French windows and plunged at Bourton into the open air.
note: Page one. A June morning in London tips Clarissa back to being eighteen and throwing open a window in the country. Woolf's method in miniature: the present and a memory in the same breath.

text: …She felt very young; at the same time unspeakably aged. She sliced like a knife through everything; at the same time was outside, looking on. She had a perpetual sense, as she watched the taxi cabs, of being out, out, far out to sea and alone; she always had the feeling that it was very, very dangerous to live even one day.
note: Clarissa, in her fifties, waiting to cross a street. Woolf names a feeling most of us have and few can describe: being inside your life and watching it from outside at the same time.

text: …If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence. As it is, the quickest of us walk about well wadded with stupidity.
note: The narrator steps out of the story to say something about all of us: we survive only because we don't feel the full weight of ordinary sorrow. One of the most quoted passages in Victorian fiction.

text: …Here and there a cygnet is reared uneasily among the ducklings in the brown pond, and never finds the living stream in fellowship with its own oary-footed kind.
note: From the Prelude, before the story begins. Eliot's image for a person born with more ambition than her world has room for. It's the question the whole novel asks.

text: …E com pequeno esforço, sendo o titulo seu, poderá cuidar que a obra é sua. Ha livros que apenas terão isso dos seus autores; alguns nem tanto.
note: The narrator has just explained his nickname, which a young poet on the train gave him after he dozed off during the poet's recital. A sly joke about authorship on the very first page.
translation: …And with a little effort, since the title is his, he may imagine the work is his too. There are books that owe no more than that to their authors; some not even that.

text: O meu fim evidente era atar as duas pontas da vida, e restaurar na velhice a adolescencia. Pois, senhor, não consegui recompor o que foi nem o que fui. Em tudo, se o rosto é egual, a physionomia é differente. Se só me faltassem os outros, vá; um homem consola-se mais ou menos das pessoas que perde; mas falto eu mesmo, e esta lacuna é tudo.
note: Why he is writing the book: to tie the two ends of his life together. Machado fits a whole philosophy of memory and ageing into one paragraph.
translation: My evident aim was to tie together the two ends of life, and to restore adolescence in old age. Well, sir, I did not manage to recompose what was, nor what I was. In everything, though the face is the same, the expression is different. If it were only others I lacked, so be it; a man consoles himself, more or less, for the people he loses; but I myself am missing, and this gap is everything.

text: …Olhos de ressaca? Vá, de ressaca. É o que me dá ideia daquella feição nova. Traziam não sei que fluido mysterioso e energico, uma força que arrastava para dentro, como a vaga que se retira da praia, nos dias de ressaca.
note: As a teenager, the narrator searches for words to describe Capitu's eyes. “Olhos de ressaca” (undertow eyes) became one of the most famous images in Brazilian literature.
translation: …Undertow eyes? Yes, undertow. That is what gives me the idea of that new look of hers. They held some mysterious, energetic fluid, a force that dragged one inward, like the wave that pulls back from the beach on days of heavy surf.

text:
AO VERME
QUE
PRIMEIRO ROEU AS FRIAS CARNES
DO MEU CADAVER
DEDICO
COMO SAUDOSA LEMBRANÇA
ESTAS
MEMÓRIAS PÓSTHUMAS
note: The dedication page: dark, funny, and unlike anything else in nineteenth-century fiction. You know exactly what kind of book this is before chapter one.
translation:
TO THE WORM
WHO
FIRST GNAWED THE COLD FLESH
OF MY CORPSE
I DEDICATE
AS A FOND REMEMBRANCE
THESE
POSTHUMOUS MEMOIRS

text: …a primeira é que eu não sou propriamente um autor defunto, mas um defunto autor, para quem a campa foi outro berço; a segunda é que o escripto ficaria assim mais galante e mais novo.
note: Brás Cubas explains why his memoirs begin with his death. The wordplay “autor defunto / defunto autor” barely survives translation, and the joke sets the tone for the whole novel.
translation: …the first is that I am not exactly a writer who has died, but a dead man who writes, for whom the grave was a second cradle; the second is that the writing would thus be more elegant and more novel.

text: …Escrevi-a com a penna da galhofa e a tinta da melancholia; e não é difficil antever o que poderá sair desse connubio.
note: From the note “To the reader”. Possibly the best one-line description of Machado's style ever written, and he wrote it himself.
translation: …I wrote it with the pen of mockery and the ink of melancholy; and it is not hard to foresee what may come of such a union.

text: It was said that a new person had appeared on the seafront: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney’s pavilion, he saw, walking on the seafront, a fair-haired young lady of medium height, wearing a beret; a white Pomeranian dog was running behind her.
note: The first paragraph of Chekhov's most famous story: a rumour, a seafront, a bored man paying attention. Nothing has happened yet, and everything is set up.

text: …There ought to be behind the door of every happy, contented man someone standing with a hammer continually reminding him with a tap that there are unhappy people; that however happy he may be, life will show him her laws sooner or later, trouble will come for him—disease, poverty, losses, and no one will see or hear, just as now he neither sees nor hears others.
note: A man has just visited his brother, who finally got the little farm he dreamed of all his life. Instead of feeling glad for him, he is overcome by this thought.

text: At first the weather was fine and still. The thrushes were calling, and in the swamps close by something alive droned pitifully with a sound like blowing into an empty bottle. A snipe flew by, and the shot aimed at it rang out with a gay, resounding note in the spring air. But when it began to get dark in the forest a cold, penetrating wind blew inappropriately from the east, and everything sank into silence. Needles of ice stretched across the pools, and it felt cheerless, remote, and lonely in the forest. There was a whiff of winter.
note: The opening of a four-page story. Watch the weather turn halfway through the paragraph, and the mood turn with it.

text:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:…
note: The ode's first lines. Keats describes a feeling so strong it is almost painful, then reveals a few lines later that it comes from being too happy, listening to a bird.

text:
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun;
Conspiring with him how to load and bless
With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eaves run;…
note: The opening of Keats's last great poem. No complaint about decline: just fullness, ripeness, abundance.

text:
Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard
Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on;
Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear’d
Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone:…
note: Looking at musicians painted on an ancient vase, Keats argues that the music we imagine is sweeter than any we can hear.
